title: Captain MacWhirr in the Typhoon
text:
Captain MacWhirr of the steamer Nan-Shan was a man of so little imagination that his crew thought him dull. He read facts, not ideas, and took everything literally. On one voyage in the China Sea, carrying about two hundred Chinese laborers returning home with their savings in camphorwood chests, the barometer began to fall faster than anyone had seen.

His first mate, Jukes, suggested changing course to put the ship's head to the swell and run around the storm, as the books advised. MacWhirr refused. Steering away would make them late, and the storm might go anywhere. He would not go around a gale. The way to get through it was to face it.

The typhoon struck with stunning force. The bridge was smashed, the boats were torn away, and Jukes, clinging on beside the captain, felt the end was near. Below, the laborers' chests broke open, their silver dollars spilled across the hold, and the men fought each other in the darkness. MacWhirr sent Jukes and the crew down to stop the fighting, gather up the money and lash the men safely in place. He held the ship steady through the eye of the storm and the second blow.

The Nan-Shan reached port battered but afloat. Since no one could tell whose dollars were whose, MacWhirr divided the money equally among the laborers. Jukes wrote to a friend, grudgingly, that the captain had got out of it very well for such a stupid man.
lesson: In a crisis, steady attention to the next necessary task often matters more than brilliance. Face the problem, protect people, and solve fairness questions in a way everyone can accept.
people: Captain MacWhirr, Jukes, the crew of the Nan-Shan
location: England (story set in the China Sea)
